analysis.one_liner: Lets companies decide which investor disclosures are 'material' and restricts proxy advisors and index fund voting.
analysis.headline: The House Financial Services Committee reported the bill on a near-party-line 27-24 vote on June 24, 2026, and it now sits on the House calendar awaiting a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill rewrites the rules around how public companies disclose information and how shareholder votes work. It would let each company decide for itself whether information is 'material' before it has to disclose it, create an SEC advisory committee made up of company executives, and impose new registration, reporting, and legal-liability requirements on proxy advisory firms — the firms that tell big investors how to vote company shares. It would ban automated voting that just follows a proxy advisor's recommendation, and require index funds to either follow individual investors' instructions, follow the company board's recommendation, abstain, or mirror other shareholders. It also requires investors to give informed consent before an adviser can weigh non-financial factors like environmental or social concerns in personalized advice.
analysis.who_benefits: Public companies gain the most: they would decide for themselves whether required disclosures are 'material,' face less pressure from shareholder proposals, and gain a formal advisory committee at the SEC drawn from their own executives and professional advisers. Companies would also get new tools to challenge proxy advisory firms, including the right to see and correct the data behind voting recommendations before they are published and a private right of action against firms that endorse proposals later found illegal.

how_it_helps.text: When the SEC writes any new disclosure rule, companies would only have to disclose information they themselves have determined is material to a voting or investment decision, under a standard the bill writes into the Securities Act and the Exchange Act [S2][S3].

A new Public Company Advisory Committee would advise the SEC on disclosure, governance, and proxy rules; at least half its members must be officers or directors of public companies, with the rest drawn from industry associations and advisers like lawyers and bankers, and it would be exempt from the Federal Advisory Committee Act's open-meeting rules [S3].

Proxy advisory firms would have to register with the SEC, certify their advice serves investors' 'best economic interest,' disclose their methods and conflicts, and give companies they rate advance access to the data behind recommendations plus an ombudsman process before publication; firms would be liable to issuers for costs if they endorsed a proposal later found to violate law [S2][S3].

Passively managed funds (index funds) could no longer vote shares on non-routine matters at their own discretion; they must follow the beneficial owner's instructions, follow the company board's recommendation, abstain, or mirror other shareholders' votes, and they get a broad liability safe harbor for doing so [S2][S3].

Advisers and brokers giving personalized advice must determine the customer's best interest using pecuniary (financial) factors, which cannot be subordinated to non-financial factors unless the customer gives informed consent [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Investors, including the retirement savers whose money is invested through index funds and 401(k)s, would receive less information: a company could keep out of its disclosures anything it decides is not material, and the public and competitors could not independently judge that call. Proxy advisory firms bear heavy compliance, reporting, and litigation costs. Large asset managers lose discretion over how they vote trillions of dollars of shares on non-routine matters, and brokers and advisers offering values-based portfolios face a new consent requirement and disclosure of the financial costs of doing so.
analysis.who_pays_short: Investors, proxy advisors, and large asset managers

drawbacks.text: The materiality provision shifts the line between what must and need not be disclosed to the company itself; the 'reasonable investor' standard is judged at the time of the company's own determination, so investors and analysts lose the ability to rely on a uniform, regulator-set floor of disclosure [S3].

The Public Company Advisory Committee's membership is drawn from public company officers, industry associations, and their outside advisers, with no requirement to include investor representatives, and its meetings are exempt from federal open-committee rules [S3].

The issuer-facing private right of action and pre-publication correction requirements could make proxy advisory firms more cautious or more expensive, reducing the research that funds — including pension and 401(k) funds — rely on to vote shares [S3].

Supporters' strongest good-faith case cuts the other way: automated voting that follows a proxy advisor without review can put millions of small savers' shares behind policies they never chose, and the bill's requirements that passive funds follow investor instructions or abstain respond to a real complaint about index fund voting power [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a genuine mix of mechanisms but its center of gravity favors the companies being regulated over the people who own them. The bans on robovoting and on outsourcing voting decisions, and the requirement to honor small investors' voting instructions, address real problems for savers. But the same bill hands companies the power to self-certify what disclosures are 'material,' seats company executives on a new SEC advisory body, and arms issuers with new legal claims against the firms that scrutinize them. On balance, investors get a modest voice upgrade and a significant information downgrade; public companies come out well ahead.

outcome.mechanism: The committee passed it on a narrow 27-24 vote in April, formally reported it to the House on June 24, and it has been sitting on the House calendar without a floor vote since.

narrative.text: Rep. Bryan Steil (R-WI) introduced the bill on April 15, 2026, together with Rep. Ann Wagner, and it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee [S1][S3][S5].
The committee held a markup on April 21 and ordered the bill reported on a roll call of 27 to 24 [S5].

On June 24, 2026, the committee formally reported an amended version as H. Rept. 119-712, and the bill was placed on the Union Calendar (No. 618), the list of bills awaiting House floor action; Rep. Dan Meuser joined as an additional sponsor that day [S3][S5].
The bill has attracted two Republican cosponsors and no Democratic cosponsors [S4].

The CRS summary confirms the bill limits what public companies must disclose to what they determine is material, restricts proxy advisory firms, bans robovoting, and sets out the four options (instructions, board recommendation, abstain, mirror) for passively managed funds [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing has finally changed yet: the bill cleared committee but has not been voted on by the full House. To the extent anything has shifted, public companies are closer to getting what they asked for — less mandatory disclosure and more leverage over the proxy firms and index funds that hold them accountable — while investors' existing disclosure and voting rules remain in place for now only because the bill has not moved further.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor and its only two cosponsors are Republicans [S4], and the committee advanced it on a 27-24 vote, consistent with the committee's Republican majority working its will and Democrats opposed [S5].

industries.note: Companies would decide for themselves which disclosures are material, gain an advisory committee at the SEC drawn from their own executives, and get new rights and legal claims against proxy advisory firms. The cost is borne by the investors, including retirement savers, who rely on that disclosure to judge where their money goes.

industries.industry: Proxy advisory firms (e.g., the firms that advise pension and mutual fund voting)
industries.note: The bill requires SEC registration, annual reporting, conflict-of-interest rules, pre-publication review by the companies being rated, and issuer lawsuits over endorsed proposals. These firms' interests here run alongside ordinary savers', since their voting research is what funds holding 401(k) and pension money rely on; heavier liability could narrow that advice or raise its price.

industries.industry: Large asset managers and index funds
industries.note: Managers of $100 billion or more must perform a documented economic analysis for each shareholder proposal they vote on and file detailed annual reports on their proxy advisor use, and passive funds lose discretion to vote shares freely on non-routine matters. Whether that restrains outsized index fund influence that savers never chose, or strips the main check on corporate boards, is the core dispute the bill embodies; the bill also shields fund managers from liability for votes cast the new way.

industries.industry: Brokers and advisers offering values-based (ESG) portfolios
industries.note: Personalized advice must be based on financial (pecuniary) factors, and non-financial factors like environmental or social preferences cannot be considered without the customer's informed consent, plus disclosure of the potential financial cost. The friction falls on advisers whose customers want values-aligned portfolios.

industries.industry: U.S. multinationals subject to EU sustainability rules
industries.note: The bill directs the SEC to study the 'detrimental impact' of the EU's Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence and Reporting Directives and recommend mitigating measures, building a record against rules that require such companies to report supply-chain environmental and human-rights impacts.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has a narrow partisan committee majority behind it and only two cosponsors. Bills like this sometimes reach the House floor under a rule after a calendar wait, but with no visible Democratic support the likely path is a House floor vote at most, followed by inaction in the Senate and the bill dying when this Congress ends on January 3, 2027.
